scotus.text: On February 20, 2026, in Learning Resources v. Trump, the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs.

atmus.text: On March 4, 2026, the Court of International Trade ordered refunds of IEEPA duties on unliquidated entries and on liquidated entries that are not yet final, for importers whether or not they sued.
atmus.note: Appendix A named the case Atmus Filtration and said the order included interest. The source names no case and says the order did not mention interest; interest comes from statute and CAPE (see cape-interest).

cape-phase1.text: CBP's CAPE refund process opened April 20, 2026 for unliquidated entries and entries within 80 days of liquidation.

cape-phase3.text: CAPE Phase 3 opened October 6, 2026 for finally liquidated entries under court-ordered reliquidation, only for Court of International Trade plaintiffs who provided a valid importer number by July 30, 2026.

cape-totals.text: As of October 2, 2026, about $126 billion in refunds had been transmitted to Treasury, and about $1.1 billion was held for importers missing ACH bank details.

limitations.text: Suits at the Court of International Trade have a two-year limitations period from the date of deposit, so entries from early 2025 start expiring around February 2027.
limitations.note: Troutman says the two years run from the date of deposit. Bradley and GingerControl describe the clock as running from accrual.

class.text: On October 8, 2026 the Court of International Trade certified a class in Freestyle World v. CBP covering importers of record who paid IEEPA duties from February 1, 2025 to February 19, 2026 and did not separately sue. Certification does not yet order refunds. A schedule is due October 22, 2026.

ddp.text: On delivered-duty-paid courier shipments the courier is often the importer of record, but the entry summary (CBP Form 7501) is what confirms it. Only the importer of record or the broker that filed the entries can file a CAPE claim.
ddp.note: Corrects Appendix A, which said the courier is always the importer of record and the merchant has no standing. The source says DDP alone does not decide who the importer is, and refunds can go to an eligible designated recipient.

ieepa-ch99.text: IEEPA duties show up under their own Chapter 99 codes on the CBP Form 7501 entry summary and on the courier or broker duty invoice.
ieepa-ch99.note: From the build spec; GingerControl confirms. No source gives the 9903 heading numbers.

protest-deadline.text: A liquidated entry can be protested within 180 days of liquidation.
protest-deadline.note: From the build spec's question 5; three cited sources confirm the 180-day window.

s301.text: Section 301 forced-labor tariffs took effect July 24, 2026, at 10% or 12.5% depending on the country. Lawsuits challenging them were filed the same day.

s301-10.text: The 10% Section 301 forced-labor rate applies to Canada, Mexico, the EU, the UK, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan and others.
s301-10.note: Akerman calls its list illustrative. Clark Hill's proposal listed India at 12.5%; Akerman, after the tariffs took effect, lists India at 10%.

s301-125.text: The 12.5% Section 301 forced-labor rate applies to China, Vietnam, Thailand, Japan, Korea, Brazil and more than 40 others.

s232-metals.text: Since April 6, 2026, Section 232 tariffs are 50% on steel, aluminum and copper articles and 25% to 50% on derivatives.

s232-autos.text: Section 232 tariffs on autos and auto parts are 25%.

s232-trucks.text: Section 232 tariffs are 25% on medium and heavy trucks and parts, and 10% on buses.

s232-lumber.text: Section 232 tariffs on timber and lumber are 10%.

s232-furniture.text: Section 232 tariffs on upholstered furniture, kitchen cabinets and vanities are 25% now. Under Proclamation 11000 they rise on January 1, 2027 to 30% for upholstered furniture and 50% for kitchen cabinets and vanities.
s232-furniture.note: Covington's table still shows the increase taking effect January 1, 2026; Proclamation 11000 (91 FR 1039) delays it to January 1, 2027.

de-minimis.text: The de minimis exemption has been suspended for all countries since August 29, 2025, anchored by interim final rules published June 24, 2026 for all modes other than international mail. The statutory repeal takes effect July 1, 2027.

mpf-min.text: The minimum merchandise processing fee is $26.79 per entry.
mpf-min.note: Appendix A says $26.79 per entry. The source calls it the informal entry minimum, and the page shows no date. Confirm with the broker which entries it covers. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.
mpf-min.assumption: We apply the $26.79 minimum merchandise processing fee to every shipment. Our source describes it as the minimum for informal entries, so formal entries can pay more.

ach-required.text: CBP pays refunds electronically through ACE, so ACH bank details must be on file. About $1.1 billion was being held for importers missing them as of October 2, 2026.

protest-blocks-cape.text: An entry with an open protest is not eligible for CAPE in any phase.
protest-blocks-cape.note: Not in Appendix A. Troutman only; Baker Tilly said open-protest handling was under development (July 15). Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.
protest-blocks-cape.assumption: That an open protest makes an entry ineligible for CAPE comes from one law firm's analysis (Troutman). CBP was still building its handling of open protests in July 2026.

protest-recommended.text: Several law firms (Bradley, BakerLaw and Troutman) recommend protective protests while the 180-day window is open. Troutman also notes that the Court of International Trade held in AGS v. CBP that IEEPA duty collection is not protestable.
protest-recommended.note: Not in Appendix A. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.

cape-filing.text: CAPE claims are filed in the ACE Secure Data Portal by the importer of record or the broker that filed the entries, so ACE access is required. Setting up ACE access can take from a few business days to about six weeks.
cape-filing.note: Not in Appendix A. Sources disagree on ACE setup time: Baker Tilly says up to six weeks, GingerControl says 3 to 5 business days. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.

s301-exemptions.text: USMCA-compliant goods of Canada or Mexico, and articles and parts subject to Section 232, are exempt from the Section 301 forced-labor tariffs.
s301-exemptions.note: In Appendix A, but only Clark Hill's description of the June 2026 proposal mentions these exemptions. Akerman, writing after the tariffs took effect, does not. Akerman also mentions 471 exempt products. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.
s301-exemptions.assumption: We assume the Section 301 forced-labor tariff does not apply to USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada or Mexico, or to goods already under Section 232, as the June 2026 proposal said. We could not confirm this in the final action. If it does not hold, add the country's Section 301 rate (10% or 12.5%).

s301-more-countries.text: Akerman's lists of countries at each rate, published after the tariffs took effect, include at 10%: Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Jordan, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago; at 12.5%: Australia, Saudi Arabia and Switzerland.
s301-more-countries.note: Not in Appendix A. Once confirmed, add these countries to the calculator picklist. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.
s301-more-countries.assumption: Rates for these countries come from Akerman's list, which it calls illustrative. Clark Hill's description of the June 2026 proposal put Honduras, India, Jordan, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago at 12.5% instead of 10%.

s301-net-of-mfn.text: For the EU and Taiwan (10%) and for Japan, Korea and Switzerland (12.5%), the Section 301 forced-labor rate is net of the MFN base duty.
s301-net-of-mfn.note: Not in Appendix A. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.
s301-net-of-mfn.assumption: For goods from the EU, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland, we treat the Section 301 rate as including the base duty, so only the difference is added. This comes from one source (Akerman).

s232-country-deals.text: Section 232 actions include country-specific provisions for the UK, EU, Japan and Korea, and Proclamation 11000 excepts countries that reach an agreement.
s232-country-deals.note: Not in Appendix A. No rates given. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.
s232-country-deals.assumption: Section 232 terms for goods from the UK, EU, Japan and South Korea can differ under trade agreements. We use the standard rate because the sources give no country rates.

s232-semis.text: A 25% Section 232 tariff on specified advanced computing chips and their derivatives took effect January 15, 2026. Other semiconductors are left to negotiations.
s232-semis.note: Not in Appendix A. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.

broker-fee-range.text: A cost example puts customs broker fees at $25 to $75 per entry.
broker-fee-range.note: Not in Appendix A. Decided by Joe and Claude on October 16, 2026 without broker review; shown to users with an assumption footnote where it is one.
broker-fee-range.assumption: When you do not enter your broker's fee, we use $25 to $75 per entry, from one published cost example. Your broker's actual fee may differ.

semis-other.text: Section 232 tariffs do not yet cover semiconductors other than specified advanced computing chips; those are left to negotiations.
semis-other.assumption: We assume no Section 232 tariff on semiconductors other than specified advanced computing chips, since the source says the rest are left to negotiations.

no-path-dates.title: Likely no refund path

summary.text: The IEEPA refunds cover duties paid on imports from February 1, 2025 to February 19, 2026. You said you did not import in that window, so there is likely nothing to refund.

summary: If a supplier or courier handled imports for you in that window, check with them before ruling it out.

no-path-not-ieepa.title: Likely no refund path

summary.text: The Supreme Court ruling covers tariffs charged under IEEPA. Section 232 and Section 301 tariffs are separate and still in effect, so they are not part of these refunds.

summary: If you are not sure which tariffs you paid, your broker can tell you which lines on your entries were IEEPA duties.

courier.title: Start with your courier

summary.text: On delivered-duty-paid courier shipments, the courier is often the importer of record. The entry summary (CBP Form 7501) or the courier's duty invoice shows who it was.
Only the importer of record or the broker that filed the entries can file a CAPE claim.

steps: Ask UPS, FedEx or DHL who was the importer of record on your shipments, and how they are handling IEEPA refunds.
Ask whether any refund on your shipments will be passed back to you.
If your company was the importer of record on some entries, run these questions again for those.
documents: Tracking numbers and dates for shipments from February 1, 2025 to February 19, 2026
The duty and tax invoices the courier billed you

find-importer.title: First, find out who was the importer of record

summary.text: On delivered-duty-paid courier shipments, the courier is often the importer of record. The entry summary (CBP Form 7501) shows who it was.

steps: Ask your customs broker who was the importer of record on your entries since February 1, 2025.
Then run these questions again with that answer.

deadlines.text: Do not wait long. The time to sue at the Court of International Trade runs two years from the date the duty was deposited, so entries from early 2025 start expiring around February 2027.

own-suit.title: Your own Court of International Trade case

summary.text: Because you filed your own suit, your refund runs through that case. The Freestyle World class covers importers who did not separately sue.

steps.text: If any entries are finally liquidated, confirm with your counsel that your importer number was provided by July 30, 2026. CAPE Phase 3 covers finally liquidated entries only for plaintiffs who did that.
Ask your broker whether your unliquidated entries, and entries within 80 days of liquidation, went through CAPE.

documents: Your case number and your counsel's contact
Your entry numbers and entry summaries since February 1, 2025

cape.title: CAPE refund through your broker

summary.text: CBP's CAPE refund process has covered unliquidated entries, and entries within 80 days of liquidation, since April 20, 2026.
The Court of International Trade ordered refunds on unliquidated entries and on liquidated entries that are not yet final, whether or not the importer sued.

steps: Ask your broker whether your entries have gone through CAPE and where each refund stands.

steps.text: CAPE claims are filed in ACE by the importer of record or the broker that filed the entries, so make sure one of you has ACE access.

steps: Match the refunds that land in your bank account against the amounts your broker reports.
documents: Your entry numbers and entry summaries since February 1, 2025
Your broker's invoices showing the duty paid
Your company's bank details for ACH

deadlines.text: If an entry is not refunded through CAPE, the time to sue at the Court of International Trade runs two years from the date the duty was deposited. Entries from early 2025 start expiring around February 2027.

cape-or-protest.title: CAPE or a protest, through your broker

summary.text: CAPE covers entries within 80 days of liquidation. Entries liquidated earlier than that are outside CAPE's first phase.
The Court of International Trade ordered refunds on liquidated entries that are not yet final.

Law firms differ on protests. Several recommend protective protests while the 180-day window is open; one Court of International Trade decision (AGS v. CBP) held that IEEPA duty collection is not protestable.

steps: Ask your broker which entries are still within 80 days of liquidation and whether they went through CAPE.
For the rest, ask your broker whether to file a protest, and the protest deadline for each entry.

steps.text: An entry with an open protest is not eligible for CAPE, so check CAPE first for any entry that might still qualify.

documents: Your entry numbers, entry summaries and liquidation dates since February 1, 2025
Your broker's invoices showing the duty paid

deadlines.text: A liquidated entry can be protested within 180 days of liquidation.

deadlines: Protest deadlines run from each entry's liquidation date, so ask your broker about them this week.

steps: Ask whether any entries without a protest can still go through CAPE.

summary.text: Since October 6, 2026, CAPE has covered finally liquidated entries for Court of International Trade plaintiffs who provided an importer number by July 30, 2026. You said you did.

steps: Confirm with your counsel that your importer number was provided by July 30, 2026.
Ask your broker to confirm your finally liquidated entries are in CAPE Phase 3, and where each refund stands.

class.title: The Freestyle World class action

summary.text: Your entries are finally liquidated. CAPE covers finally liquidated entries only for court plaintiffs who provided an importer number by July 30, 2026.

On October 8, 2026 the Court of International Trade certified a class in Freestyle World v. CBP for importers of record who paid IEEPA duties from February 1, 2025 to February 19, 2026 and did not separately sue. Certification does not order refunds yet, and a schedule is due October 22, 2026.

steps: Keep your entry records together so you can move quickly if the class wins refunds.

steps.text: Ask a trade attorney whether to rely on the class or file your own suit. The class covers importers who did not sue separately, so filing your own suit means relying on that suit instead.

documents: Your entry numbers and entry summaries since February 1, 2025
Your broker's invoices showing the IEEPA duty paid
